Formula Laboratory

Essential Formulas from All Lectures

Lecture 2: Portfolio Theory

1. Expected Return

$$ E(r) = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i r_i $$
Logic: Probability weighted average of all outcomes.
Constraint: $\sum p_i = 1$

2. Variance & Standard Deviation

$$ \sigma^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i (r_i - E[r])^2 $$ $$ \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2} $$
Logic: Expected squared deviation from the mean. Measure of total risk.

3. Covariance & Correlation

$$ Cov(r_A, r_B) = \sum p_i (r_{A,i} - E[r_A])(r_{B,i} - E[r_B]) $$ $$ \rho_{AB} = \frac{Cov(r_A, r_B)}{\sigma_A \sigma_B} $$
Range: Correlation $\rho \in [-1, 1]$.
Positive = Move together. Negative = Diversification benefit.

4. Portfolio Variance (2 Assets)

$$ \sigma_p^2 = w_A^2 \sigma_A^2 + w_B^2 \sigma_B^2 + 2 w_A w_B \rho_{AB} \sigma_A \sigma_B $$
Critical: Don't forget the covariance term ($2 w_A w_B \sigma_{AB}$)!

5. Sharpe Ratio (CAL Slope)

$$ SR = \frac{E(r_p) - r_f}{\sigma_p} $$
Meaning: Excess return (Risk Premium) per unit of risk.

Lecture 3: Efficient Frontier

6. Minimum Variance Portfolio (MVP) Weights

$$ w_A = \frac{\sigma_B^2 - \rho_{AB}\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\rho_{AB}\sigma_A\sigma_B} $$ $$ w_B = 1 - w_A $$
Use: Find the portfolio with minimum risk (leftmost point on efficient frontier).

Lecture 4: CAPM

7. Beta

$$ \beta_i = \frac{Cov(r_i, r_m)}{Var(r_m)} = \frac{\rho_{i,m} \sigma_i \sigma_m}{\sigma_m^2} = \rho_{i,m} \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_m} $$
Meaning: Sensitivity to market movements. $\beta = 1$ means moves with market.

8. CAPM (Security Market Line)

$$ E(r_i) = r_f + \beta_i [E(r_m) - r_f] $$
Components: $r_f$ = risk-free rate, $E(r_m) - r_f$ = market risk premium.

9. Alpha (Mispricing)

$$ \alpha_i = E(r_i) - [r_f + \beta_i(E(r_m) - r_f)] $$
Interpretation: $\alpha > 0$ = underpriced (buy), $\alpha < 0$ = overpriced (sell).

10. Capital Market Line (CML)

$$ E(r_p) = r_f + \frac{E(r_m) - r_f}{\sigma_m} \sigma_p $$
Note: CML applies only to efficient portfolios (combinations of market portfolio and risk-free asset).

Lecture 5&6: Bond Valuation

11. Bond Price

$$ P = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+y)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+y)^T} $$
Variables: $C$ = coupon payment, $F$ = face value, $y$ = YTM, $T$ = maturity.

12. Macaulay Duration

$$ D = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} t \cdot PV(CF_t)}{P} $$
Meaning: Weighted average time to receive cash flows (weights = PV of each CF).

13. Modified Duration

$$ D_{mod} = \frac{D}{1+y} $$ $$ \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod} \times \Delta y $$
Use: Approximate percentage price change for small yield changes.

14. Forward Rate

$$ (1+s_n)^n = (1+s_{n-1})^{n-1}(1+f(n-1,n)) $$
Meaning: $f(n-1,n)$ is the implied forward rate from year $n-1$ to year $n$.

Lecture 7: Stock Valuation

15. Gordon Growth Model

$$ P_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g} $$
Requirement: $g < r$ (growth rate must be less than required return).

16. PVGO Decomposition

$$ P_0 = \frac{E_1}{r} + PVGO $$
Components: No-growth value + Present value of growth opportunities.

17. P/E Ratio

$$ \frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1}{r} + \frac{PVGO}{E_1} $$
Insight: Higher P/E indicates higher growth expectations (larger PVGO).

Lecture 8: Capital Budgeting

18. Net Present Value (NPV)

$$ NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} = -C_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} $$
Rule: Accept if NPV > 0, reject if NPV < 0.

19. Internal Rate of Return (IRR)

$$ NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{CF_t}{(1+IRR)^t} = 0 $$
Rule: Accept if IRR > cost of capital. But use NPV for mutually exclusive projects.

20. Profitability Index (PI)

$$ PI = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}}{C_0} = \frac{PV(Future\,CFs)}{Initial\,Investment} $$
Rule: Accept if PI > 1. Useful for capital rationing (rank by PI).

      • APV = V_U + PV(ITS)

      • PV(ITS) = τ×D (permanent debt at r_D)

    • FTE Method
      • FTE: Discount Equity Cash Flows at r_E
      • FTE = PV(FCFE) discounted at r_E
      • FCFE = FCF − After-tax Interest + Net Borrowing
      • Use When: Focus on Equity Value
    • Method Comparison
      • All Three Methods Give Same V_L
      • WACC: Constant D/E, Simplest
      • APV: Fixed Debt Schedule
      • FTE: Shareholder Focus
    • Unlevered Cost of Capital
      • Pre-tax WACC = r_U (constant D/E)
      • r_U = (E/V)·r_E + (D/V)·r_D

Step-by-step logic for common Exam Problems

Lecture 2: Portfolio Theory

L2 Essential
Problem: GlobalWealth Asset Management is constructing a diversified portfolio for a high-net-worth client who wants exposure to both US and Japanese equity markets. The client has expressed concerns about volatility and wants to understand the risk-reduction benefits of international diversification.

The portfolio manager proposes allocating 60% to US stocks and 40% to Japanese stocks. Historical data shows:
• US Stocks: Expected return = 13.6%, Standard deviation = 15.4%
• Japanese Stocks: Expected return = 15.0%, Standard deviation = 23.0%
• Correlation between the two markets: ρ = 0.27

Calculate the Portfolio Standard Deviation to demonstrate the diversification benefit to the client.
Formula: σP2 = w12σ12 + w22σ22 + 2w1w2ρ12σ1σ2
Note: We calculate Variance (σ2) first, then Square Root for Stdev.
Term 1 (US): 0.62 * 0.1542 = 0.36 * 0.023716 = 0.008538
Term 2 (JP): 0.42 * 0.232 = 0.16 * 0.0529 = 0.008464
Term 3 (Interaction): 2 * 0.6 * 0.4 * 0.27 * 0.154 * 0.23
= 0.48 * 0.27 * 0.03542
= 0.004590
Variance: 0.008538 + 0.008464 + 0.004590 = 0.021592
Standard Deviation: √0.021592 = 0.1469 (or 14.69%)

Check: Is it lower than the weighted average risk? Yes (Diversification works).
L2 Essential
Problem: RetireWell Financial Advisors is helping a 45-year-old client plan for retirement. The client has a moderate risk tolerance and wants to achieve a target return of 12% on their retirement portfolio.

The advisor has identified a diversified risky portfolio (Portfolio P) with an expected return of 15% and standard deviation of 22%. The current risk-free rate (Treasury bills) is 7%.

How much should the client invest in the Risky Portfolio (w) versus the Risk-Free Asset to achieve the target return?
Combined E(r) = w * E(rP) + (1-w) * rf
We know E(r)=0.12, E(rP)=0.15, rf=0.07. Solve for w.
0.12 = w(0.15) + 0.07 - 0.07w
0.12 - 0.07 = w(0.15 - 0.07)
0.05 = w(0.08)
w = 0.05 / 0.08 = 0.625 (or 62.5%)
Invest 62.5% in Risky Portfolio P.
Invest 37.5% in Risk-Free Asset (T-bills).

Lecture 3: Efficient Frontier

L3 Essential
Problem: Vanguard Portfolio Solutions is constructing a minimum-risk portfolio for a conservative institutional investor. The investment committee has narrowed down the universe to two stocks: Stock A (a stable utility company) and Stock B (a volatile tech company).

Historical volatility data shows:
• Stock A: Standard deviation = σA = 20%
• Stock B: Standard deviation = σB = 30%
• Correlation between A and B: ρ = 0.3

Find the optimal weights (wA and wB) that minimize portfolio variance.
$$ w_A = \frac{\sigma_B^2 - \rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B} $$
Numerator: 0.302 - 0.3(0.20)(0.30) = 0.09 - 0.018 = 0.072
Denominator: 0.202 + 0.302 - 2(0.3)(0.20)(0.30) = 0.04 + 0.09 - 0.036 = 0.094
wA = 0.072 / 0.094 = 0.766 (76.6%)
wB = 1 - 0.766 = 0.234 (23.4%)

Lecture 4: CAPM

L4 Essential
Problem: BlackRock Equity Research is evaluating Stock X, a mid-cap technology company, for potential inclusion in their actively managed fund. The stock has a beta of 1.2, indicating higher volatility than the market.

Current market conditions:
• Risk-free rate (10-year Treasury): 3%
• Market expected return (S&P 500): 10%
• Stock X analyst forecast return: 12%

Calculate the CAPM expected return and alpha to determine if Stock X is underpriced or overpriced.
$$ E(r_X) = r_f + \beta_X[E(r_m) - r_f] $$ $$ E(r_X) = 0.03 + 1.2(0.10 - 0.03) = 0.03 + 1.2(0.07) = 0.03 + 0.084 = 0.114 $$ CAPM Expected Return = 11.4%
$$ \alpha = Actual - CAPM = 12\% - 11.4\% = 0.6\% $$ Alpha = +0.6% (Positive alpha → Stock is underpriced → BUY)

Lecture 5&6: Bond Valuation

L5 Essential
Problem: PIMCO Fixed Income is evaluating a corporate bond issued by TechCorp Industries for their bond fund. The bond was issued two years ago and has the following characteristics:

• Face Value: \$1,000
• Coupon Rate: 6% (annual)
• Remaining Maturity: 3 years
• Current Market YTM: 5%

Since issuance, interest rates have declined, and the bond is now trading at a premium. Calculate the fair market price of this bond.
Annual Coupon = 6% × \$1,000 = \$60
Year 1: \$60
Year 2: \$60
Year 3: \$60 + \$1,000 = \$1,060
PV(Year 1) = \$60 / 1.05 = \$57.14
PV(Year 2) = \$60 / 1.052 = \$54.42
PV(Year 3) = \$1,060 / 1.053 = \$915.51
Bond Price = \$57.14 + \$54.42 + \$915.51 = \$1,027.07
Note: Price > Par because Coupon Rate (6%) > YTM (5%) → Premium bond.

Lecture 7: Stock Valuation

L7 Essential
Problem: Fidelity Dividend Growth Fund is analyzing SteadyPay Utilities, a mature electric utility company with a long history of stable dividend payments. The company operates in a regulated market with predictable cash flows.

Dividend data:
• Current Dividend (just paid): D0 = \$2.00
• Expected perpetual growth rate: g = 5%
• Required return (based on company risk): r = 12%

Calculate the fair value of SteadyPay's stock using the Gordon Growth Model.
$$ D_1 = D_0 \times (1+g) = 2.00 \times 1.05 = \$2.10 $$
$$ P_0 = \frac{D_1}{r-g} = \frac{2.10}{0.12 - 0.05} = \frac{2.10}{0.07} = \$30.00 $$ Stock Price = \$30.00

Lecture 8: Capital Budgeting

L8 Essential
Problem: InnovateTech Manufacturing is evaluating a new automated production line that would replace their aging manual equipment. The CFO has prepared a cash flow analysis for the board of directors.

Project details:
• Initial Investment: \$10,000
• Year 1 Cash Flow: \$4,000
• Year 2 Cash Flow: \$5,000
• Year 3 Cash Flow: \$4,000
• Company's cost of capital: 10%

Calculate the NPV and determine whether InnovateTech should proceed with the investment.
PV(Year 1) = \$4,000 / 1.10 = \$3,636.36
PV(Year 2) = \$5,000 / 1.102 = \$4,132.23
PV(Year 3) = \$4,000 / 1.103 = \$3,005.26
Total PV = \$3,636.36 + \$4,132.23 + \$3,005.26 = \$10,773.85
NPV = \$10,773.85 - \$10,000 = \$773.85
NPV = \$773.85 > 0 → ACCEPT the project.
The project adds \$773.85 in value.

Lecture 9: Payout Policy

L9 Essential
Problem: AppleCorp has 100 million shares outstanding at a price of \$50 per share. The firm announces a \$2 per share cash dividend. Assume perfect capital markets (no taxes, no transaction costs).

(a) What is the stock price on the ex-dividend date?
(b) A shareholder owns 1,000 shares and does NOT want cash — she wants to maintain her investment value. How many shares must she buy back after the dividend to replicate a zero-payout policy (homemade dividend reversal)?
In perfect markets, stock price falls by exactly the dividend on the ex-date:
$P_{ex} = P_{cum} - Div = \$50 - \$2 = \$48$
Intuition: The firm paid out \$2/share in cash, so firm value drops by exactly that amount.
Before dividend: 1,000 × \$50 = \$50,000
After dividend: Cash received = 1,000 × \$2 = \$2,000; Stock value = 1,000 × \$48 = \$48,000
Total = \$48,000 + \$2,000 = \$50,000 ✓ (Wealth unchanged — MM irrelevance)
She received \$2,000 cash. To reinvest it at \$48/share:
Shares to buy = \$2,000 / \$48 = 41.67 shares
New holding = 1,000 + 41.67 = 1,041.67 shares × \$48 = \$50,000 ✓
Conclusion: Investors can undo any payout policy themselves — hence MM dividend irrelevance.

Lecture 10: Payout Policy (II)

L10 Essential
Problem: DividendCo currently pays a dividend of \$2.00 per share. According to the Lintner Model, the firm targets a 40% payout ratio and uses a speed of adjustment (SOA) = 0.3. This year, earnings per share are \$8.00.

What dividend will DividendCo pay this year?
Target Dividend = Target Payout Ratio × EPS
= 0.40 × \$8.00 = \$3.20
Lintner Model: $\Delta Div = SOA \times (Div^* - Div_{t-1})$
= 0.3 × (\$3.20 − \$2.00) = 0.3 × \$1.20 = \$0.36
New Dividend = \$2.00 + \$0.36 = \$2.36
Key insight: Firms smooth dividends — they do NOT jump immediately to the target. SOA < 1 reflects dividend smoothing behavior documented by Lintner (1956).

Lecture 11: Capital Budgeting (I)

L11 Essential
Problem: TechVentures Inc. is evaluating a new product line. The project requires an initial investment of \$500,000 and generates the following incremental cash flows:

• Year 1: Revenue \$400,000; Cash Costs \$200,000; Depreciation \$100,000; Tax rate 30%
• Year 2: Revenue \$500,000; Cash Costs \$220,000; Depreciation \$100,000; Tax rate 30%
• Year 2 also requires a \$50,000 increase in NWC (recovered at end of Year 2)
• Cost of capital: 12%

Calculate the project FCF for each year and the NPV.
FCF = (Revenue − Costs − Depreciation) × (1 − τ) + Depreciation − CapEx − ΔNWC
= Unlevered Net Income + Depreciation − CapEx − ΔNWC
EBIT = \$400,000 − \$200,000 − \$100,000 = \$100,000
Unlevered NI = \$100,000 × (1 − 0.30) = \$70,000
FCF₁ = \$70,000 + \$100,000 − \$0 − \$0 = \$170,000
EBIT = \$500,000 − \$220,000 − \$100,000 = \$180,000
Unlevered NI = \$180,000 × 0.70 = \$126,000
FCF₂ = \$126,000 + \$100,000 − \$0 − \$50,000 + \$50,000 (NWC recovery) = \$226,000
NPV = −\$500,000 + \$170,000/1.12 + \$226,000/1.12²
= −\$500,000 + \$151,786 + \$180,165
= −\$168,049 → REJECT the project.

Lecture 12: Capital Budgeting (II) — WACC vs APV

L12 Advanced
Problem: Avco Manufacturing is evaluating a project with the following data:

• Unlevered FCF: Year 1 = \$3.0M, Year 2 = \$3.0M, Year 3 = \$3.0M
• Unlevered cost of capital: r_U = 10%
• Firm maintains D/V = 50% (constant leverage)
• Cost of debt: r_D = 6%; Tax rate: τ = 40%

(a) Find V_U using APV Step 1. (b) Find PV(ITS) assuming constant D/E (discount ITS at r_U). (c) Find V_L.
V_U = PV of FCFs discounted at r_U = 10%
= \$3.0M/1.10 + \$3.0M/1.10² + \$3.0M/1.10³
= \$2.727M + \$2.479M + \$2.254M = \$7.46M
With constant D/E, ITS risk = project risk → discount at r_U = 10%
D each year = 50% × V_L (unknown, but we use the shortcut):
PV(ITS) = τ × r_D × D / r_U ... but with constant D/E, use:
PV(ITS) = τ_c × D = 0.40 × (50% × V_L)
Solving: V_L = V_U + 0.40 × 0.50 × V_L → V_L × (1 − 0.20) = \$7.46M
V_L = \$7.46M / 0.80 = \$9.33M
PV(ITS) = V_L − V_U = \$9.33M − \$7.46M = \$1.87M
D = 50% × \$9.33M = \$4.67M; PV(ITS) = τ × D = 0.40 × \$4.67M = \$1.87M ✓

Lecture 13: Capital Budgeting (III) — Project Risk

L13 Advanced
Problem: ConglomerateCorp (D/E = 1.0, r_D = 5%) wants to evaluate a new division in the retail sector. It finds a pure-play retail comparable, RetailPure Inc., with:

• Equity beta: β_E = 1.5
• D/E ratio: 0.5 (assume β_D ≈ 0)
• Risk-free rate: r_f = 3%; Market risk premium: MRP = 6%

ConglomerateCorp has D/E = 1.0 and r_D = 5%, τ = 30%.
Find the appropriate r_WACC for the retail project.
β_U = β_E / (1 + D/E) = 1.5 / (1 + 0.5) = 1.5 / 1.5 = 1.0
This is the asset beta for the retail sector.
β_E (project) = β_U × (1 + D/E) = 1.0 × (1 + 1.0) = 2.0
r_E (project) = r_f + β_E × MRP = 3% + 2.0 × 6% = 15%
D/V = D/(D+E) = 1/(1+1) = 0.5; E/V = 0.5
r_WACC = (E/V)·r_E + (D/V)·r_D·(1−τ)
= 0.5 × 15% + 0.5 × 5% × (1 − 0.30)
= 7.5% + 1.75% = 9.25%
Use 9.25% to discount the retail project FCFs — not ConglomerateCorp's own WACC.

Lecture 14: Capital Budgeting (IV) — Information Asymmetry & Mispricing

L14 Advanced
Problem (Gap Inc. Case): Gap Inc. is considering a store expansion project requiring \$100M initial investment. Management knows the true risk warrants a 5% discount rate, but outside investors (due to information asymmetry) demand 6% for providing expansion capital. The project generates \$8M annual FCF in perpetuity. Tax rate = 25%.

Calculate:
(a) NPV using management's true cost of capital (5%)
(b) NPV using investors' required return (6%)
(c) The cost of information asymmetry (mispricing cost)
PV of perpetuity = C / r = $8M / 0.05 = $160M
NPV (true value) = \$160M − \$100M = +$60M
This is what the project is really worth to existing shareholders
PV at investors' rate = $8M / 0.06 = $133.33M
NPV (at 6%) = \$133.33M − \$100M = +$33.33M
If financed at 6%, new investors capture value at the expense of old shareholders
Mispricing cost = NPV(true) − NPV(6%)
= $60M − $33.33M = $26.67M

Alternatively: Value transferred to new investors
= \$160M − \$133.33M = $26.67M

New investors pay \$100M for securities worth \$133.33M to them, but the firm gives up claims worth \$160M at true value. The \$26.67M difference is wealth transferred from old to new shareholders.
Should Gap proceed with the expansion?

From firm perspective: Yes, NPV = +$60M > 0
From existing shareholders perspective: No!

If financed externally at 6%:
• Existing shareholders gain: \$33.33M (their share of the 6%-based NPV)
• But they lose \$26.67M in value transferred to new investors
• Net gain: \$33.33M − \$26.67M = only $6.67M

Pecking Order Theory insight: Gap should prefer internal financing or debt (less information-sensitive) over equity to minimize this mispricing cost.

Lecture 15: Mergers & Acquisitions — Valuation & Synergies

L15 Core
Problem: AcquirerCo is evaluating a friendly acquisition of TargetInc. Current market data:
• TargetInc: 10M shares outstanding at \$40/share (pre-announcement)
• AcquirerCo: 50M shares outstanding at \$80/share
• Expected synergies: \$200M (present value)
• Acquisition premium offered: 25% above Target's current price

Calculate:
(a) Target's standalone value and acquisition offer price
(b) Total value created and its distribution
(c) Exchange ratio if using all-stock payment
Target Standalone Value:
= 10M shares × \$40/share = $400M

Offer Price (with 25% premium):
= \$40 × 1.25 = $50 per share
Total consideration = 10M × \$50 = $500M

Premium paid = \$500M − \$400M = \$100M
Combined Firm Value (post-merger):
= Acquirer value + Target standalone + Synergies
= (50M × \$80) + \$400M + \$200M
= \$4,000M + \$400M + \$200M = $4,600M

Pre-merger combined value:
= \$4,000M + \$400M = $4,400M

Total value created (synergies): $200M
Value captured by Target shareholders:
= Premium received = \$500M − \$400M = $100M

Value captured by Acquirer shareholders:
= Synergies − Premium = \$200M − \$100M = $100M

Distribution: 50% to Target / 50% to Acquirer
This is a "fair" deal where both parties share the synergy gains equally.
All-Stock Payment Structure:

Exchange ratio based on offer price:
= Offer price / Acquirer share price
= \$50 / \$80 = 0.625 shares of Acquirer per Target share

New shares issued:
= 10M Target shares × 0.625 = 6.25M new shares

Post-merger ownership:
• Old Acquirer shareholders: 50M / 56.25M = 88.9%
• Ex-Target shareholders: 6.25M / 56.25M = 11.1%

Target shareholders receive \$500M worth of Acquirer stock (6.25M × \$80)
Combined firm value: $4,600M (from Step 2)
Total shares outstanding: 56.25M

Post-merger share price:
= \$4,600M / 56.25M = $81.78 per share

Value gain for Acquirer shareholders:
= \$81.78 − \$80.00 = +$1.78 per share (+2.2%)

Value gain for Target shareholders:
Received 0.625 × \$81.78 = \$51.11 worth per original share
vs. their original \$40 = +$11.11 per share (+27.8%)

Note: Target shareholders actually gain more than 25% premium due to share price appreciation from synergies!

Concept Check

Self-Test: Definitions and Logic

Lecture 1: Introduction

1. Why is the goal "Maximize Profit" problematic compared to "Maximize Stock Price"?
Analysis:
  • Short-termism: "Profit" (Earnings) can be manipulated by cutting R&D or maintenance, which boosts today's numbers but hurts future value ($PV$).
  • Risk Ignorance: Profit accounting does not explicitly account for risk ($\sigma^2$).
  • The Solution: Stock Price ($P_0$) incorporates the present value of all future cash flows adjusted for risk.
2. What is the Agency Problem and how does "Entrenchment" fit in?
Definition: A conflict of interest where Managers (Agents) prioritize their own utility over Shareholders' (Principals) wealth.

Entrenchment: Managers take actions to make themselves difficult to fire (e.g., Poison Pills, Staggered Boards). This allows them to extract private benefits (perks, empire building) without fear of discipline from the board or market.

Lecture 2: Portfolio Theory

3. Explain the Mean-Variance Criterion for dominance.
Definition: For a risk-averse investor, Asset A dominates Asset B if: $$ E(r_A) \ge E(r_B) \quad \text{and} \quad \sigma_A^2 < \sigma_B^2 $$
— OR —
$$ E(r_A) > E(r_B) \quad \text{and} \quad \sigma_A^2 \le \sigma_B^2 $$ In simple terms: You typically choose A if it offers higher return for the same risk, or lower risk for the same return.
4. In the Utility function $U = E(r) - 0.5 A \sigma^2$, what happens if $A$ increases?
Analysis:
  • $A$ represents the Coefficient of Risk Aversion.
  • If $A$ increases, the penalty term ($-0.5 A \sigma^2$) becomes more negative.
  • Result: The investor requires a much higher Expected Return ($E(r)$) to accept the same amount of risk ($\sigma^2$). The Indifference Curve becomes steeper.

Lecture 3: Efficient Frontier

5. Explain the Separation Property (Two-Fund Theorem).
Statement: All investors, regardless of their risk preferences, will hold the same optimal risky portfolio (the tangency portfolio).

Implication: Investors differ only in how they allocate between:
  • Fund 1: The optimal risky portfolio (tangency portfolio)
  • Fund 2: The risk-free asset
Risk-averse investors hold more of the risk-free asset; risk-tolerant investors hold more (or even leverage) the risky portfolio.
6. What is the difference between systematic and unsystematic risk?
Systematic Risk (Market Risk):
  • Risk that affects all assets (e.g., recession, interest rate changes, inflation)
  • Cannot be diversified away
  • Measured by beta ($\beta$)
  • Is priced in equilibrium (investors demand compensation)
Unsystematic Risk (Firm-Specific Risk):
  • Risk unique to individual assets (e.g., management changes, product recalls)
  • Can be diversified away by holding many assets
  • Not priced in equilibrium (no compensation)

Lecture 4: CAPM

7. What is the difference between the SML and CML?
Security Market Line (SML):
  • Plots: Expected Return vs. Beta ($\beta$)
  • Applies to: All assets (efficient or not)
  • Formula: $E(r_i) = r_f + \beta_i[E(r_m) - r_f]$
  • Risk measure: Systematic risk only
Capital Market Line (CML):
  • Plots: Expected Return vs. Standard Deviation ($\sigma$)
  • Applies to: Efficient portfolios only (combinations of market portfolio and risk-free asset)
  • Formula: $E(r_p) = r_f + \frac{E(r_m)-r_f}{\sigma_m}\sigma_p$
  • Risk measure: Total risk
8. How do you interpret Alpha ($\alpha$)?
Definition: $\alpha = E(r_i) - [r_f + \beta_i(E(r_m) - r_f)]$

Interpretation:
  • $\alpha > 0$: Stock plots above the SML → Underpriced → BUY
  • $\alpha = 0$: Stock is on the SML → Fairly priced
  • $\alpha < 0$: Stock plots below the SML → Overpriced → SELL
Alpha represents abnormal return (return not explained by systematic risk).

Lecture 5&6: Bond Valuation

9. What is the difference between Duration and Maturity?
Maturity:
  • Time until the bond's principal is repaid
  • Simple calendar measure
Duration (Macaulay Duration):
  • Weighted average time to receive all cash flows
  • Weights = Present value of each cash flow
  • Always ≤ Maturity (except for zero-coupon bonds where Duration = Maturity)
  • Better measure of interest rate risk
Modified Duration: $D_{mod} = \frac{D}{1+y}$ → Used to approximate price sensitivity to yield changes.
10. Explain Forward Rates and the Expectations Hypothesis.
Forward Rate: The implied future interest rate embedded in current spot rates.
Example: $f(1,2)$ is the rate from year 1 to year 2, calculated from: $(1+s_2)^2 = (1+s_1)(1+f(1,2))$

Expectations Hypothesis:
  • Forward rates equal expected future spot rates
  • No risk premium for holding longer-term bonds
  • Upward-sloping yield curve → Market expects rates to rise
Liquidity Preference Theory: Adds a liquidity premium to forward rates (investors prefer short-term bonds).

Lecture 7: Stock Valuation

11. What are the key assumptions of the Gordon Growth Model?
Gordon Growth Model: $P_0 = \frac{D_1}{r-g}$

Key Assumptions:
  • Constant growth: Dividends grow at constant rate $g$ forever
  • $g < r$: Growth rate must be less than required return (otherwise model explodes)
  • Stable firm: Best for mature, stable companies with predictable dividends
  • Dividends paid: Company must pay dividends (not suitable for non-dividend stocks)
Limitations: Not suitable for high-growth firms, firms with volatile dividends, or non-dividend-paying stocks.
12. What does PVGO tell us about a company?
PVGO Decomposition: $P_0 = \frac{E_1}{r} + PVGO$

Components:
  • $\frac{E_1}{r}$: No-growth value (if all earnings paid as dividends)
  • PVGO: Present value of growth opportunities (value from reinvesting earnings at returns > $r$)
Interpretation:
  • High PVGO: Growth stock (most value from future projects)
  • Low/Zero PVGO: Mature stock (value from current earnings)
  • Negative PVGO: Company destroys value by reinvesting (should pay out all earnings)
P/E Ratio: $\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1}{r} + \frac{PVGO}{E_1}$ → Higher P/E indicates higher growth expectations.

Lecture 8: Capital Budgeting

13. Why is NPV superior to IRR for mutually exclusive projects?
NPV Advantages:
  • Measures absolute value added: NPV shows dollar value created
  • Realistic reinvestment assumption: Assumes cash flows reinvested at cost of capital
  • Additive: NPVs of independent projects can be summed
  • No multiple IRR problem: Always gives unique answer
IRR Problems:
  • Unrealistic reinvestment: Assumes reinvestment at IRR itself
  • Scale problem: Ignores project size (small project with high IRR vs. large project with lower IRR)
  • Timing problem: Doesn't properly account for timing differences
  • Multiple IRRs: Non-conventional cash flows can have multiple IRRs
Rule: When NPV and IRR conflict, always use NPV.
14. What are the limitations of the Payback Period method?
Payback Period: Time required to recover initial investment.

Major Limitations:
  • Ignores time value of money: Treats all cash flows equally regardless of timing
  • Ignores cash flows after payback: A project with huge cash flows after payback looks the same as one with none
  • Ignores risk: No adjustment for project risk
  • Arbitrary cutoff: No theoretical basis for choosing payback threshold
When useful: As a rough liquidity measure or for very risky projects where distant cash flows are highly uncertain.

Discounted Payback: Addresses time value issue but still ignores cash flows after payback.

Lecture 9: Payout Policy

15. Explain MM Dividend Irrelevance. What is a "homemade dividend"?
MM Dividend Irrelevance (Perfect Markets): In perfect capital markets (no taxes, no transaction costs, no asymmetric information), payout policy does not affect firm value. Investors care only about total return, not how it is split between dividends and capital gains.

Homemade Dividend:
  • If a firm pays too little dividend, an investor can sell shares to create their own cash flow.
  • If a firm pays too much dividend, an investor can reinvest the dividend by buying more shares.
  • Result: Investors can replicate any payout policy themselves → firm's payout choice is irrelevant.
Key Assumption: Breaks down with taxes (dividends taxed higher than capital gains), transaction costs, or asymmetric information.
16. Why might firms prefer share repurchases over dividends from a tax perspective?
Tax Advantage of Repurchases:
  • Dividends are taxed as ordinary income when received — investor has no choice.
  • Repurchases create capital gains, which are: (1) taxed at a lower rate, and (2) only realized when the investor chooses to sell (tax timing option).
Tax-Adjusted Preference: $\frac{1 - \tau_{div}}{1 - \tau_{cg}} < 1$ when $\tau_{div} > \tau_{cg}$ → repurchases dominate.

Clientele Effect: High-tax investors prefer low/no dividends; tax-exempt investors (pension funds) are indifferent.

Flexibility: Repurchases are also more flexible — firms can reduce them without the negative signal that a dividend cut sends.

Lecture 10: Payout Policy (II)

17. What is the Lintner Model and what does it tell us about dividend smoothing?
Lintner Model (1956): $$\Delta Div_t = SOA \times (Div^* - Div_{t-1})$$ where $Div^* = $ Target Payout Ratio $\times$ EPS, and SOA = Speed of Adjustment (0 < SOA < 1).

Key Insights:
  • Firms do not immediately jump to the target dividend — they adjust gradually.
  • Low SOA (e.g., 0.2) = very smooth dividends; High SOA (e.g., 0.8) = rapid adjustment.
  • Managers are reluctant to cut dividends → they only raise dividends when confident earnings are permanently higher.
Why smooth? Dividend cuts signal bad news → stock price drops sharply. Smoothing avoids this negative signal.
18. How do agency costs motivate payout policy? Connect to the Free Cash Flow problem.
Free Cash Flow (FCF) Problem: When firms generate more cash than they have positive-NPV projects, managers may waste it on:
  • Empire building (overpriced acquisitions)
  • Excessive perks and compensation
  • Negative-NPV investments
Payout as Discipline: Paying out excess cash (via dividends or repurchases) reduces FCF under managerial control → reduces agency costs of equity.

Microsoft Example: In 2004, Microsoft had \$60B+ in cash with limited high-return investments. Announcing a \$100B repurchase + dividend increase reduced agency costs and boosted the stock price by ~80% over 4 years.

Lecture 11: Capital Budgeting (I)

19. What are "incremental cash flows"? Why must we exclude sunk costs but include opportunity costs?
Incremental Cash Flows: The change in the firm's total cash flows that results directly from taking the project.

Sunk Costs (Exclude):
  • Already spent and unrecoverable regardless of the decision.
  • Example: \$500K already spent on R&D — irrelevant to whether to launch the product.
  • Including sunk costs leads to the "sunk cost fallacy" — throwing good money after bad.
Opportunity Costs (Include):
  • The value of the next-best alternative foregone.
  • Example: Using a warehouse you own for a project — you forgo rental income. That rental income is a cost of the project.
Externalities / Cannibalization: Also include — if a new product steals sales from an existing product, that lost revenue is an incremental cost.
20. How do you calculate Free Cash Flow (FCF) for capital budgeting? What role does depreciation play?
FCF Formula: $$FCF = \underbrace{(Revenue - Costs - Dep) \times (1-\tau)}_{\text{Unlevered Net Income}} + Dep - CapEx - \Delta NWC$$
Depreciation's Dual Role:
  • Reduces taxes: Depreciation is tax-deductible → lowers taxable income → tax shield = $\tau \times Dep$
  • Added back: Not a real cash outflow, so added back after computing after-tax income.
  • Net effect: $+\tau \times Dep$ (the depreciation tax shield)
NWC: Increases in NWC (e.g., more inventory) are cash outflows; decreases (project wind-down) are cash inflows.

Lecture 12: Capital Budgeting (II)

21. Compare the WACC, APV, and FTE methods. When should you use each?
All three methods give the same $V_L$ in theory.

Method Discount Best When
WACC FCF at $r_{WACC}$ Constant D/E ratio; simplest
APV FCF at $r_U$, then add PV(ITS) Fixed debt schedule; complex financing
FTE FCFE at $r_E$ Focus on equity value; leveraged buyouts

Key distinction — ITS discount rate:
  • Constant D/E → ITS has same risk as firm → discount at $r_U$
  • Fixed debt schedule → ITS is certain → discount at $r_D$
22. What is the unlevered cost of capital $r_U$ and how do you calculate it from observable data?
Unlevered Cost of Capital ($r_U$): The required return on the firm's assets as if it were all-equity financed. It reflects only business risk, not financial risk.

Formula (Pre-tax WACC, assumes constant D/E): $$r_U = \frac{E}{D+E} \cdot r_E + \frac{D}{D+E} \cdot r_D$$ Note: This uses pre-tax $r_D$ (no tax adjustment), unlike after-tax WACC.

Why it matters:
  • APV method discounts unlevered FCF at $r_U$
  • Used to unlever/re-lever betas for project risk adjustment
  • $r_U$ is the same for all firms in the same industry (same business risk)

Lecture 13: Capital Budgeting (III)

23. How do you adjust for project risk when a project is in a different industry than the firm?
Pure-Play Comparable Approach:
  1. Find comparables: Identify publicly traded firms in the same industry as the project.
  2. Unlever their betas: $\beta_U = \frac{\beta_E}{1 + D/E}$ (assuming $\beta_D \approx 0$)
  3. Average $\beta_U$ across comparables to get the project's business risk.
  4. Re-lever at the firm's own target D/E: $\beta_E^{project} = \beta_U \times (1 + D/E_{firm})$
  5. Compute project $r_E$ via CAPM, then project $r_{WACC}$.
Key insight: Use the project's industry risk, not the firm's overall WACC. A steel company evaluating a software project should use software industry betas.
24. What is the difference between a fixed debt schedule and a constant D/E ratio? How does this affect the APV calculation?
Constant D/E Ratio:
  • Firm rebalances debt as firm value changes → debt level is uncertain (tied to firm value)
  • ITS has same risk as firm → discount ITS at $r_U$
  • Use WACC method (simplest)
Fixed Debt Schedule:
  • Debt amounts are predetermined (e.g., LBO with fixed repayment schedule)
  • ITS is known with certainty → discount ITS at $r_D$ (lower rate → higher PV of ITS)
  • Use APV method
Practical impact: Fixed debt → higher PV(ITS) than constant D/E → higher $V_L$. The difference can be significant for highly leveraged transactions.

Lecture 14: Capital Budgeting (IV) — Information Asymmetry & Mispricing

25. What limitation do WACC, APV, and FTE methods share that Lecture 14 addresses?
The Perfect Market Assumption:

All three valuation methods (WACC, APV, FTE) assume securities are fairly priced — investors pay exactly what the securities are worth in equilibrium.

L14 relaxes this: In reality, information asymmetry means management knows more about the firm's true prospects than outside investors. This causes:
  • Adverse selection (Lemons Problem): Outside investors cannot distinguish good from bad firms, so they price all securities at an average → good firms are underpriced, bad firms are overpriced.
  • Mispricing cost: If a firm issues underpriced securities (e.g., equity at too low a price), new investors capture value at the expense of existing shareholders.
Key insight: Even if a project has positive NPV under fair pricing, it may destroy value for existing shareholders if financed with underpriced new equity.
26. What is "mispricing cost" and how does it affect a project's adjusted NPV?
Mispricing Cost Defined:

Mispricing cost = value given up by existing shareholders when new securities are issued at a price below their true (intrinsic) value.

$$\text{Mispricing Cost} = \text{True Value of Securities Issued} - \text{Price Received}$$ Effect on project value: $$NPV_{\text{adjusted}} = NPV_{\text{true}} - \text{PV(Mispricing Cost)}$$ Example intuition (Gap Inc.):
  • True cost of capital: 5% → project worth $160M → true NPV = +$60M
  • Investors demand 6% (due to info asymmetry) → they value the securities at $133M
  • Mispricing cost = $160M − $133M = $26.67M (transferred to new investors)
  • Adjusted NPV to existing shareholders = $60M − $26.67M = only $33.33M
Policy implication (Pecking Order): Firms prefer retained earnings → then debt → then equity, to avoid issuing underpriced securities.
27. Why might a firm with a positive-NPV project choose not to invest if it must use external equity financing?
The Myers-Majluf "Underinvestment" Problem:

When information asymmetry is severe, issuing new equity can be so costly (due to mispricing) that it wipes out the project's NPV for existing shareholders — even if the project is genuinely valuable.

Logic chain:
  1. Market believes the firm may be overvalued → prices new equity below its true value.
  2. Existing shareholders absorb the dilution cost (mispricing cost).
  3. If mispricing cost > project NPV → firm rationally passes up a positive-NPV project.
Solution:
  • Use internal funds (no information problem)
  • Use debt (less information-sensitive than equity)
  • Build financial slack to avoid needing costly external equity
Real-world signal: Equity issuance announcements typically cause stock prices to fall (~3%) — markets interpret it as a signal that management believes the stock is overvalued.

Lecture 15: Mergers & Acquisitions

28. What are the three types of mergers? Give one strategic reason for each.
Three Merger Types:
  1. Horizontal Merger — Combines firms in the same industry.
    • Reason: Achieve economies of scale, eliminate a competitor, gain pricing power.
    • Example: Two automakers merging to reduce production costs.
  2. Vertical Merger — Combines firms at different stages of the supply chain.
    • Reason: Secure input supply, reduce transaction costs, capture margin from supplier/distributor.
    • Example: An oil company acquiring a network of petrol stations.
  3. Conglomerate Merger — Combines firms in unrelated industries.
    • Reason: Diversify revenue streams, deploy excess cash, enter new growth markets.
    • Example: A tobacco company acquiring a food company.
Key exam note: Horizontal mergers attract the most antitrust regulatory scrutiny because they reduce direct competition.
29. Compare cash vs. stock payment in an acquisition. Which is better for the acquirer when synergies are uncertain?
Cash Payment:
  • Target shareholders receive a fixed, certain amount regardless of future performance.
  • Acquirer bears all the risk that synergies may not materialise.
  • Target shareholders pay capital gains tax immediately.
  • Signals acquirer confidence (willing to pay a fixed price).
Stock Payment:
  • Target shareholders receive acquirer shares → they share in post-merger upside and downside.
  • Risk is shared between acquirer and target shareholders.
  • Target shareholders can defer capital gains tax (tax-free reorganisation).
  • Signals acquirer may believe its own stock is overvalued (negative signal).
When synergies are uncertain: Stock payment is better for the acquirer — if synergies disappoint, the acquirer gives away fewer real resources since the stock it issued is also worth less. Cash would have locked in a full premium with no offset.
30. What are synergies in M&A? How is the value of synergies calculated, and who typically captures it?
Synergies defined: Additional value created by combining two firms that neither could achieve independently. $$V_{\text{synergy}} = V_{\text{combined}} - V_{\text{acquirer}} - V_{\text{target (standalone)}}$$ Sources of synergies:
  • Revenue synergies: Cross-selling, expanded customer base, new markets.
  • Cost synergies: Eliminating duplicate functions, economies of scale in purchasing.
  • Financial synergies: Lower cost of capital from size, unused debt capacity, tax benefits.
Value distribution:
  • Target shareholders capture: the acquisition premium (offer price above standalone value).
  • Acquirer shareholders capture: synergies minus the premium paid.
  • If premium = full synergy value → acquirer captures nothing; target gets all gains.
Empirical fact: On average, target shareholders gain ~25–30% in acquisitions; acquirer shareholders on average gain close to zero — they tend to overpay (winner's curse / hubris).

📝 Exam Tips — Midterm

🧮 BA II Plus
Ready 0
TVM
CF / NPV / IRR

💡 Pro Tips

TVM Basics:

  • Cash inflows = positive, outflows = negative
  • $I/Y$ = per-period rate. If annual rate with semi-annual compounding, divide by 2
  • $N$ = total number of periods (years × frequency)

Bond Valuation:

  • $N$ = years to maturity × coupon frequency
  • $I/Y$ = YTM ÷ coupon frequency
  • $PMT$ = coupon payment per period
  • $FV$ = face value (usually 1000)
  • Solve for $PV$ = bond price (negative = cash out)

Loan Amortization:

  • $PV$ = loan amount (positive)
  • $FV$ = 0 (fully amortized)
  • Solve for $PMT$ (negative = payment out)

NPV / IRR:

  • $CF_0$ is usually negative (initial investment)
  • NPV > 0 → accept project
  • IRR > required return → accept project

🗺️ Learning Path ＋
What it is: Your personalised study roadmap across all 8 lectures.

How to use:
  • The Overview shows your overall progress and per-lecture completion bars.

  • Click Go → on each step to jump to the relevant module. The step is automatically marked ✅.
  • A 🗺️ button appears in the top-right corner so you can return to your exact position at any time.
  • Once a lecture is 100% complete, a 🔄 Restart button appears to reset its progress.
💡 Recommended starting point if you're new to this tool.
🎯 Quiz Mode ＋
What it is: A randomised exam simulator with 60 questions covering L1–L8.

How to use:
  • Filter by lecture using the Topic dropdown, or leave it on "All" for a mixed set.
  • Set the number of questions, then click Start Quiz.
  • After submitting, each question shows the correct answer and a detailed explanation.
  • Wrong answers are automatically saved to the Wrong Answers module.
  • For questions linked to the Knowledge Map, click Review in Tree to see the concept in context.
💡 Includes both MCQ and Debug-type questions. Debug questions ask you to identify the incorrect step in a worked solution.
🔄 Review ＋
What it is: A spaced-repetition review queue that surfaces questions you need to revisit.

How to use:
  • Questions you answered incorrectly are queued here for follow-up review.
  • Work through the queue and mark each question as correct or incorrect again.
  • The system tracks your streak — answer correctly 3 times in a row to "master" a question.
💡 Use this module regularly (e.g. daily) to reinforce weak areas before exams.
📕 Wrong Answers ＋
What it is: A personal error log with accuracy analytics and a knowledge radar chart.

How to use:
  • View your overall accuracy, total attempts, and weakest lecture at a glance.
  • The radar chart visualises your relative strength across all lectures.
  • Scroll down to see every question you got wrong, with the correct answer shown.
  • Click Jump to Question on any wrong answer to revisit it in Quiz Mode.
💡 Focus on lectures where your radar chart shows the smallest area.
📋 Templates ＋
What it is: 10 standardised problem-solving templates for the most common exam question types.

How to use:
  • Filter by category (e.g. Portfolio, CAPM, Bonds) using the dropdown.
  • Each template shows a step-by-step framework, common mistakes to avoid, and a worked example.
  • Use these as a checklist when solving exam questions under time pressure.
💡 Print or screenshot the templates most relevant to your weak areas before the exam.
🎮 Playground ＋
What it is: An interactive formula explorer where you can adjust parameters and see results update in real time.

How to use:
  • Select a formula from the dropdown (e.g. Portfolio Variance, CAPM, Bond Price).
  • Use the sliders or input fields to change parameter values.
  • The output updates instantly, helping you build intuition for how each variable affects the result.
  • Your last selected formula is remembered when you switch tabs.
💡 Try extreme values (e.g. ρ = +1 vs ρ = −1) to understand the limits of diversification.
🧮 Formula Lab ＋
What it is: A reference sheet of all 20 key formulas, organised by lecture.

How to use:
  • Browse formulas by scrolling, or jump directly to a specific formula via the Search bar or Learning Path.
  • Each card shows the formula, variable definitions, and a brief intuition note.
  • Use the 🔍 global search bar at the top to find any formula by name.
💡 Use alongside Playground to see a formula's definition and then experiment with its values.
🗺️ Knowledge Map ＋
What it is: An expandable tree diagram for each lecture showing the full concept hierarchy.

How to use:

  • Click any node with a + icon to expand its sub-concepts.
  • Use Expand All / Collapse All buttons to control the view.
  • Hover over nodes for a subtle highlight effect.
💡 Study the map before attempting Quiz Mode for that lecture — it primes your memory for the question topics.
📝 Calc Walkthrough ＋
What it is: Step-by-step worked examples for the most calculation-heavy exam questions, one per lecture.

How to use:

💡 Pay attention to the units and rounding at each step — these are common sources of exam errors.
